item.title: New Zealand: Insurance industry welcomes the Climate Change Response Amendment Bill
item.description:
Insurers in New Zealand have welcomed the Climate Change Response Amendment Bill, which sets out a long-awaited framework for climate adaptation. The industry has, however, said that funding, implementation and durable political support will be critical to turning plans into meaningful risk reduction.

A media release by the Insurance Council of New Zealand (ICNZ) said, reducing risk in vulnerable communities was critical to protecting people and supporting continued access to insurance. ICNZ Chief Executive Kris Faafoi said, “The introduction of this Bill is good to see, but the proof will be in the doing.

“Planning is important, but what insurers, councils and communities need to see now is action that reduces risk and helps protect people, property and infrastructure.” 

The Bill will require adaptation planning in the highest-risk areas, with councils required to plan how high-risk communities prepare for the impacts of climate change. Plans are expected to cover at least 30 years and set out the sequence of actions and investment needed to manage climate-driven natural hazard risks over time.

Mr Faafoi said long-term planning must be backed by long-term certainty. “Keeping communities safe from natural hazards will require sustained action and investment over many years.

“Councils need confidence that the policy framework and funding will endure beyond electoral cycles so they can make long-term decisions about reducing risk.”

“That’s why government leadership and durable cross-party support is essential. Long-term adaptation planning requires confidence that policy settings and funding arrangements will endure,” Mr Faafoi said.

He said, “The biggest challenge now is moving from planning to funded delivery. Councils will need support to identify high-risk areas, work with communities and deliver the mitigation needed to reduce risk. Some councils are already meeting this challenge, but others will need help. Councils should not be expected to face this alone.”

Mr Faafoi said the key issue for insurers is whether New Zealand takes action to reduce risk, because that is what will help protect communities and support ongoing access to insurance. We need investment in risk reduction so communities are safer and insurance is accessible in the future.

“This legislation can help provide the framework, but what matters now is urgency, practical delivery and a credible funding pathway. If we get that right, we can better protect communities from natural hazards and help keep insurance accessible for New Zealanders,” said Mr Faafoi.

item.title: Tokenized Weather Derivatives: How Climate Risk Goes Onchain - Crypto Daily
item.description:
Tokenized Weather Derivatives: How Climate Risk Goes Onchain

Weather isn’t just small talk anymore. It’s a line item. Businesses and communities live or die on whether it rains, how hot it gets, or when the wind shows up. So of course crypto folks are trying to bring that risk onchain.

This piece breaks down tokenized weather derivatives in plain English: how they work, what makes them different from old-school hedges, where the data comes from, and what could go wrong. I’ll also flag the regulatory lines and a few real pilots worth tracking right now.

If you’re skimming for the punchline: these instruments can settle fast, run 24/7, and open access. But they come with basis risk, oracle risk, and compliance headaches you can’t ignore.

Editor's note: First, the trading desks that

stayed open on weekendscaptured flow as RWA-linked derivatives kept printing volume. Second, serious oracle work finally showed up for weather and energy. I sat in on a couple of pilot reviews where the big debates weren’t about price models but about timestamps, revision policies, and collateral waterfalls. Boring details, but that’s where these markets either work or don’t. — Sophia Bennett

Tokenized weather derivatives are onchain contracts that pay out based on measurable weather conditions like rainfall, temperature, or wind speed. They’re parametric, which means they don’t look at loss receipts or claims. They look at data from an agreed source, and if the condition hits, the contract settles automatically. The goal is faster, more transparent hedging for climate-exposed risks, with global participation and programmatic payouts.

  • They use oracles to pull verified weather data onchain and trigger payouts.
  • They can reduce paperwork and settlement delay compared to traditional hedges.
  • Access can be broader, but regulation and geofencing still matter.
  • Main risks: data quality, basis mismatch, smart contract bugs, thin liquidity.

How do tokenized weather derivatives actually work?

Think of a tokenized weather derivative as a vending machine. You pre-fund it. Someone states the rule: “Pay 1 unit for every millimeter of rain below 50 mm in June at Station X” or “Pay if average temperature exceeds 35°C this week in City Y.” Then an oracle posts the relevant data. If the condition is met, the contract pays out automatically to the token holders who are supposed to receive it.

This is parametric design. No adjusters. No loss audits. Just a trigger and a payout curve. It’s fast and auditable if the data feed is clean. That’s why the oracle is everything. We’re seeing real pilots line up to supply that data. In mid-July 2026, weather firm Kweather and L1 network Flare signed a Letter of Intent to publish verified meteorological data onchain and explore parametric insurance and weather-linked derivatives. That’s exactly the kind of pipe these products need to work in practice (CoinTrust).

Under the hood, most designs lock collateral in a smart contract. The contract checks an index (say cumulative rainfall) from a specific station or model, over a specific window. If the result falls inside the payout region, funds release. Some venues do this peer-to-peer. Others run AMMs or vaults that sell structured exposure, then tokenize shares of that risk so the position is tradable.

Why not just use traditional weather hedges?

Traditional weather risk tools exist: OTC swaps, some exchange-listed futures, and parametric insurance policies. They’re proven, but they can be slow, chunky, and gated by intermediaries. Onchain versions try to flip that script with smaller tickets, faster settlement, and around-the-clock markets. That said, the trade-offs are real.

Feature OTC Weather Swaps Exchange Weather Futures Tokenized Weather Derivatives Access Institutional, bilateral Exchange members, brokers Wallet-based (often geofenced) Ticket size Large, custom Standardized, moderate Small to large, programmable Settlement speed Days to weeks Exchange cycles Near-instant after oracle finality Transparency Private terms Public specs Onchain terms, auditable Market hours Business hours Exchange hours 24/7 Data trigger Specified station/model Exchange index Oracle-specified index Counterparty risk Bilateral credit Clearinghouse Smart contract + collateral

If you need bespoke structuring, OTC still wins. If you want transparency, faster settlement, and modular exposure that plugs into treasury rails, onchain is compelling. The real question is liquidity. RWA-linked derivatives in general have seen serious attention. Market research in July 2026 pegged June’s RWA-linked derivative volume near $300 billion, with about $20 billion trading on weekends. That appetite doesn’t guarantee weather markets will boom, but it shows the broader demand for regulated, real-world-tied exposure that never sleeps (The Block).

Where does the data come from, and can you trust it?

Parametric payouts live or die by the reference data. Good design picks sources that are observable, hard to game, and finalized quickly. That can be a named meteorological station, a gridded reanalysis, a national service like the Korea Meteorological Administration, or forecast ensembles with clear release times.

The fresh development is specialized data providers bringing feeds onchain with cryptographic attestations. The Kweather and Flare pilot aims to publish verified meteorological data directly on a base layer and explore parametric insurance and derivatives on top. If that matures, onchain contracts can reference feeds with auditable provenance and latency guarantees (CoinTrust).

Designers also layer defenses: multiple feeds with quorum rules, finalization delays to catch revisions, or committees to handle disputed readings. Some protocols cap per-market exposure until the oracle proves itself across a few seasons. And when forecasts are used for anticipatory payouts, clear cutoffs are essential. We’ve actually seen anticipatory parametric programs pay before landfall in the Caribbean, releasing funds up to three days ahead for fisherfolk as a hurricane approaches. That’s offchain insurance, but it mirrors the trigger logic that onchain products aim to codify (The Insurer).

Pro tip: always read the oracle spec. Know the station IDs, coordinates, the timestamp convention, revision policy, and how disputes are handled. If it isn’t crystal clear, the basis risk is probably higher than you think.

What’s the regulatory picture in 2026?

In the United States, many weather-linked contracts fall under the umbrella of event contracts. On July 24, 2026, the CFTC issued a staff advisory reminding designated contract markets about proper self-certification and documentation for event contracts. That’s a nudge that applies to weather derivatives that list on or through those markets, and it highlights how carefully venues need to document contract design and compliance (CFTC (Staff Letters)).

For onchain venues, the reality is a patchwork. Some offerings are structured as derivatives and seek to work with regulated intermediaries. Others geofence users in certain jurisdictions and add disclosures that they’re not available to residents of specific countries. If a protocol markets contracts to U.S. persons, commodity and securities laws may apply depending on the structure. Non-U.S. markets have their own rules; some focus on insurance licensing for parametric covers, others on derivatives venue authorization.

Two takeaways keep you out of trouble: treat these like financial instruments, not arcade games, and read the venue’s compliance page. If you’re a business hedger, talk to counsel. If you’re retail, understand you might only be able to access synthetic exposure through intermediaries that handle KYC and reporting.

Who actually needs these first?

Weather risk spreads everywhere, but a few groups feel it daily. Farmers and food processors hedge heat units or rainfall to stabilize yields or drying costs. Renewable energy operators care about wind speeds and irradiance to manage production variability. Construction firms and logistics networks watch precipitation and temperature thresholds that shut down jobsites or freeze roads.

Then there are markets you might not expect. Ride-hailing and delivery apps see volume swing with storms. Live events hedge rainfall on key dates. Even miners in power markets with nodal pricing sometimes care about temperature because it sways demand, prices, and therefore operating margins.

On the humanitarian side, anticipatory payouts are gaining steam. The Caribbean regional risk pool CCRIF, working with disaster risk reduction partners, announced a parametric instrument designed to pay up to three days before a hurricane makes landfall for fisherfolk, using forecast triggers. That’s powerful because cash arrives precisely when it’s most useful. You can imagine a near-future where similar logic is codified onchain, with escrowed funds and transparent triggers that communities can audit in real time (The Insurer).

How are risk, pricing, and collateral different onchain?

Onchain, your counterparty is a smart contract plus whoever provided capital. Pricing often leans on historical distributions, blended with forecast probabilities. The catch is non-stationarity. Climate baselines are shifting. Yesterday’s 95th percentile heat day might be tomorrow’s 90th. Backtests lie if you don’t adjust.

Liquidity also behaves differently. Some risk vaults sell tranches programmatically. AMMs might quote implied odds but widen spreads under stress. That’s fine if you’re patient. It’s rough if you need to exit mid-event. The broader context is encouraging, though. RWA-linked derivative volume overall approached $300 billion in June 2026, and roughly $20 billion of that traded on weekends. That tells you participants want real-world-tied risk that stays liquid outside business hours, which fits the profile for weather exposure if venues can attract depth (The Block).

Collateral usually means stablecoins or tokenized cash equivalents. Make sure you understand the custody stack. Is collateral held in a reputable onchain vault? Is there a circuit breaker if the stablecoin depegs? If a payout is large, can the protocol source liquidity without haircutting winners? Those operational details matter as much as the math.

What should I check before I touch one of these?

Here’s a lightweight due diligence list you can actually use. None of this is advice. It’s just the boring homework that saves headaches.

  • Reference index: exact station IDs, coordinates, units, time zone, and finalization rules.
  • Oracle design: single vs multi-source, onchain attestation, dispute process, historical uptime.
  • Trigger window: start/end timestamps, observation cadence, revision policy for late data.
  • Payout curve: linear vs stepped, caps, and whether the math matches your actual losses.
  • Collateral: asset type, custody model, emergency controls, and depeg playbooks.
  • Venue risk: audits, bug bounties, admin keys, and jurisdictional access limits.
  • Liquidity: depth, spreads, and slippage under stress. Can you unwind without eating 10%?
  • Regulatory fit: your location, KYC requirements, and reporting obligations.
  • Climate drift: whether pricing adjusts for shifting baselines, not just 30-year normals.
  • Concentration: exposure caps per market to avoid one oracle glitch draining a pool.

Common Mistakes

  • Buying the wrong index. Hedging a citywide rainfall index when your risk is a specific farm 50 km away. Solution: pick the reference that actually matches your exposure, even if it costs more.
  • Ignoring finality windows. Settling on preliminary data that later revises. Solution: know the revision policy and set a buffer before payout if volatility in the data is common.
  • Underestimating liquidity risk. Assuming you can exit mid-storm. Solution: size positions for hold-to-settlement, or pre-arrange OTC exits.
  • Forgetting collateral risk. Stablecoin depegs or custodian freezes ruin clean math. Solution: read custody docs and diversify collateral where possible.
  • Overfitting backtests. Pricing off a benign decade, then getting blindsided by a regime shift. Solution: stress test with fat tails and add margin of safety.
  • Compliance blind spots. Trading from a restricted jurisdiction. Solution: check access rules and ask counsel if you’re a business user.

If you want more practical explainers and market context around onchain risk tools, Crypto Daily covers these shifts without hype. You can browse the latest at cryptodaily.co.uk.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is this insurance or a derivative?

Parametric insurance is an insurance product with a regulated carrier and policyholder protections. A weather derivative is a financial contract tied to a weather index. Onchain products can look similar in design, but the legal wrapper, capital rules, and consumer protections differ. Read the wrapper first.

What happens if the oracle feed breaks during the measurement window?

Good designs specify a fallback: secondary feeds, time-weighted averages, or manual arbitration by a pre-named committee. If there’s no documented fallback, assume higher risk and price it in, or avoid the market.

Can retail users participate?

Sometimes. Access depends on the venue’s license, geofencing, and KYC rules. Some platforms restrict these contracts to qualified users or through broker partners. Others allow small tickets via tokenized vaults but still block certain countries.

How is it taxed?

It varies by jurisdiction and wrapper. In many places, derivatives have specific tax treatment different from insurance payouts. If you’re hedging a business risk, talk to a professional about character and timing of gains or losses.

Do forecasts or observations trigger the payout?

Both exist. Observation-based triggers use stations or reanalysis after the fact. Forecast-based triggers unlock funds earlier, which is useful for preparedness. A recent Caribbean program for fisherfolk shows how anticipatory triggers can work in the real world, and similar logic can be coded onchain.

Can NFTs represent these positions?

Yes. Positions can be wrapped as transferable tokens, including NFTs for unique terms. The benefit is portability and composability. The risk is accidental transfer or regulatory confusion if a tokenized contract is traded where it shouldn’t be.

What if the weather event happens over a weekend?

Onchain markets run 24/7, and triggers post when the oracle finalizes data. With broader RWA-linked derivatives already posting significant weekend volumes, the infrastructure and appetite for off-hours risk management are there. Just confirm your venue’s settlement cadence.

item.title: Phoenix man nearly dies of heat shock. Why unhoused people are at risk - AZCentral
item.description:
Phoenix man nearly dies of heat shock. Why unhoused people are at risk

Homeless people are susceptible to the health dangers of Arizona's summer heat. Those who are newly released from jail or prison are even more vulnerable.

Three years ago, Guy Lahti was released from prison and onto the streets in the summer. Two days later, he collapsed from heat shock.

Lahti's tragedy highlights the dangers of heat shock for those who cycle between climate-controlled incarceration facilities and homelessness.

Formerly homeless people and advocates say that more society reentry programs are needed for newly released inmates, and that they can access these programs.

In an eggshell-colored room at Montecito Post Acute Care and Rehabilitation center in Mesa, a 6-foot-3 man spends most of his day in bed. Leaving it is a feat for this mobility-challenged patient, a drastic decline from his days as a skateboarder.

Except for his height — though he’s not quite as imposing horizontal as on his feet — you’d be forgiven to think that you had wandered into a teenager’s room.

Photos of friends goofing around are pinned to the wall, car models line the windowsill, the TV always plays cartoons when it’s on. Taped to the shelf, the paraphernalia — a card printed with a dead chicken, another of an astronaut with his backside exposed, a model of the birdie hand gesture — reflects a kind of humor that’s unmistakenly juvenile.

Guy Lahti is a 34-year-old giant with the mind of a child. But he wasn’t always this way.

Three years ago, heat stroke left him with permanent brain damage.

Since he was a teenager, Lahti has toggled between incarceration and homelessness. But two days after his final release in July 2023, he collapsed on the streets and never got back on his feet again.

His case isn’t just another example of Arizona’s greatest hazard, the searing heat. It’s a cautionary tale of how the lack of reentry support can make former inmates, especially those who fall straight into homelessness, uniquely vulnerable during the hottest times of the year. From being walled indoors all day to being thrust outside day in and day out, the environmental whiplash can pose dangers that veer toward life-threatening.

For it wasn’t the heat that felled Lahti — it was the shock.

Homeless people struggle with summer heat

Over 7,000 people live on the streets in Phoenix or cycle in and out of temporary shelters every night.

Homelessness and incarceration often go hand in hand — individuals who fall into one trap can get stuck in the other. Those who were formerly locked up are 10 times more likely to be homeless than the public. That’s because an incarceration record can present a barrier to employment, which can offer a steady path toward affording a place of one’s own. A good part of the challenge stems from hiring discrimination.

It’s a pernicious revolving door — unhoused people have a higher likelihood of incarceration, after which they’re often spit back out on the streets.

Former inmates are the most housing-insecure fresh after their release, twice as likely to be homeless than those who last saw the insides of a cell half a decade ago.

In the Arizona desert, the unhoused demographic has scant opportunity to duck the omnipresent face-melting, brain-broiling heat in the summer. Among the reported heat deaths in Maricopa County, half occurred among the homeless demographic.

Climate change is adding environmental chaos to an already sweltering metropolitan area. Since 1970, the average annual temperature of Phoenix has climbed 5 degrees, in part due to the urban heat island effect. The year 2024 broke records for a streak of 113 days during which the city’s temperatures shot past 100 degrees. The year before that, that number was 66 days.

“It got to the point where I just wanted to go back to prison,” said Stacey Norris, a friend of Lahti who was also formerly unhoused. “I did that a couple times. I said, ‘f--k it.’”

Among the homeless community, one group is even more vulnerable: those who just left prison or jail and are not heat acclimatized.

The Centers for Disease Control advise gradual exposure to heat over one to two weeks. In heat-acclimated individuals, sweat glands stir into action earlier, more blood flows to the skin surface, the body scales back on churning out its own heat. These physiological adaptations tend to disappear after a month of heat avoidance.

“Different people's bodies have different responses to heat as well as different types of heat,” said Ufuoma Ovienmhada, a researcher at Arizona State University who studies environmental justice and incarceration. “Even people who are young and have no pre-existing conditions can suffer from heat-related disease and mortality when it's a shock to their system.”

Public awareness is stirring on the dangers of incarceration facilities that lack cooling. But what’s under-recognized are heat’s perils to inmates newly discharged from holdings that are equipped.

The consequences of the lack of heat acclimatization are well documented among outdoor workers. According to the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, over two-thirds of heat deaths occur during a worker’s first week on the job or after an extended absence.

During Phoenix summers, the stifling walls of a cell can be a relative mercy compared with the outside elements.

Two days before Lahti’s fateful incident, he had just left Watkins Jail, an air-conditioned facility that keeps indoor temperatures between 76 and 78 degrees, according to the Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office. Lahti’s friends claimed that he was clean of drugs at the time of his episode.

The worst of heat’s outcomes are death or permanent injury, like Lahti’s. For the homeless population, those are all too common.

“The heat has a way of weeding us out and getting rid of us,” said Benjamin Jeffrey, president of the nonprofit Mobilizing America's Commitment to Veterans (MACV) Foundation and formerly unhoused. By his count, he has lost 30 of his friends in the last five years. Lahti, whose street name is Mooch, nearly numbered as one of them.

“He’s my bro,” he added. “We were all homeless in the same crowd.”

The day tragedy struck

Kelley Greene remembers the day like it was yesterday. She had accompanied Lahti, then her partner of 11 years and with whom she navigated homelessness, to the Department of Economic Security to get his SNAP card. In the two days after his release, temperatures had climbed past 105 degrees every day. The last time Lahti was outside was six months ago in late January, when he had only known winter temps in the 40s and 60s.

Lahti was feeling warm, Greene recalled, so they swung by the Circle K on Van Buren Street under the shadow of the Loop 202 freeway to get refreshments.

Greene came back with Gatorade and ice cream, but by then, her partner’s condition had deteriorated. He was acting confused and unsteady on his feet, like he was drunk.

“I knew something wasn’t right,” she remembered.

He refused the ice cream, then stumbled off in search of nothing. Half a block later, he rested on a concrete parapet, then fainted, smashing his face bloody on the pavement.

Aside from his battered left cheekbone, he “looked like he took a nap,” Greene said. She wouldn’t know until much later the extent his organs had spiraled into mortal chaos.

She ran to get help. Lahti was whisked away in an ambulance to Valleywise Health Medical Center. She wouldn’t see him for a week.

In the intensive care unit, Lathi fought for his life. His heart stopped twice, a blood clot formed in his lung, his kidneys started failing. For four minutes, his brain was starved of oxygen.

Lahti fell into a coma. He emerged a person altered. He lost part of his memory and mobility. To this day, he can’t remember his jail stint in 2023. He can no longer walk, so he uses his feet to drag himself around in a wheelchair specially made for his height.

After two months living in the hospital, Greene helped Lahti apply for AHCCCS, the state's Medicaid program, and move into Montecito assisted living. He has been there ever since.

Accessible reentry programs are needed

These days, Greene calls on Lahti several times a week, sometimes swinging by after her work at a local Goodwill store. She often brings along Norris, her new romantic partner; all of them are friendly with each other.

During one visit, Lahti rocked about on his pillow, his tattoo-covered hands cocked painfully like he froze while playing the piano. His speech was slow and slurred, as if he were trying out a foreign language.

But Greene can still understand him perfectly, almost with telepathic accuracy. Her quips always elicit from him a laugh.

“He’s always been my best friend,” she said.

Behind the smiles and giggles lie a frustration with the lack of institutional support for those mired in the cycle of homelessness and incarceration, which caused the downfall of a healthy 31-year-old male.

His friends hope that people take away from Lahti’s story the importance of heat acclimatization, and the urgency to help those stuck outdoors to cool down. That’s already a struggle for unhoused people: Cooling centers might be spread far and wide across town, requiring seekers to walk for miles in the heat to reach. They’re often chased away, accused of trespassing — including in public spaces, due to tightening restrictions and rising hostility — when they’re simply searching for shade.

Inmates need more resources such as shelter arrangements so they have a soft landing upon release, Greene and Norris said. That way, they can duck homelessness and all the dangers that come with it, including heat injury under Phoenix’s scorching sun.

The Maricopa County Sheriff’s Office partners with several agencies to offer assistance for those looking to transition back to society. Planning starts while the individual is still in custody.

This summer, the sheriff’s office also started offering free transportation directly to cooling centers or community hubs, where newly freed inmates can access other services by the state or nonprofits.

“While every effort is made to connect individuals with available resources and support, participation in reentry services is voluntary,” said a spokesperson of the sheriff’s office via email. “Ultimately, it is the individual's decision whether to accept the assistance that is offered.”

But homeless individuals and advocates dispute the impacts and reach of these programs. Ex-inmates face a mountain of challenges to access them, including missing documentation, transportation issues, bureaucratic hoops in the application process and stiff competition for limited resources.

According to interviews in a 2017 Arizona State University study, incarcerated people struggled with limited job training opportunities, savings programs and social support post release. These are also the main reasons for high recidivism rates — 29% of former detainees find themselves back at a correctional facility in three years.

“A lot of our country just doesn't have great infrastructure for returning citizens,” Ovienmhada said.

What happened to Lahti gave Greene the final push to wean off substances for good, false friends that salved her homelessness struggles but trapped her on that path. Lahti needed her to take care of him then, and she vowed never to abandon him.

Back in his room, the friends reminisced about their homeless comrades, those who died, those who are still stuck, those who have extricated themselves. Greene promised to search thrift stores for board games so her ex-lover could exercise his brain. Norris needled Lahti to work out more to beef up his core muscles.

Greene and Norris have no illusions that Lahti will fully recover, but they hold out hope he can at least move into independent living one day.

Before the visitors left, Greene gave Lahti a hug. Her actions in the last few years have already proved it, but she told him anyway, “We love you.”

Shi En Kim covers environmental issues for The Arizona Republic and azcentral. Send tips or questions toshien.kim@arizonarepublic.com.

item.title: American Nero: Why Trump is trying to burn down the National Academy of Sciences
item.description:
By Benjamin Santer | Opinion | July 26, 2026

In a post on Truth Social earlier this month, Trump claimed that the National Academy of Sciences published “fraudulent, biased, and misleading Manuals on climate change.” He has now ordered “Federal Suspension and Debarment Officials” to review the organization’s conduct.

Although he referred to multiple “Manuals,” the president’s Truth Social screed is really about a single manual: the Federal Judicial Center’s Reference Manual on Scientific Evidence. The Reference Manual serves “as a go-to document judges can use when they deal with issues involving scientific testimony.” For the first time, the most recent version of the manual  contains a climate science chapter. It describes the hard scientific evidence that fossil fuel burning is influencing extreme weather events. This science is anathema to the oil industry and to its conservative supporters, including the president, and they have responded by attacking the manual and its authors.

The Federal Judicial Center caved to a request by 27 Republican state attorneys general to remove the climate chapter from the Reference Manual, but it is still publicly available on the website of the National Academy of Sciences. This open defiance of overt political pressure is causing problems for the National Academies.

Established by President Abraham Lincoln in 1863, the National Academy of Sciences is the premier scientific organization in the United States. One part of its mission is to produce and promote “the adoption of independent, authoritative, trusted scientific advice to the government for the benefit of society.”

I’m a member of the National Academy of Sciences. I’m also a climate scientist. I’m writing this essay as a private citizen, not as a representative of the official or unofficial views of the academy. I simply care about its survival.

I’ve written and spoken about Trump’s views on climate science since 2014. In essays, op-eds, podcasts, and open letters—including an open letter to Trump himself. It’s painful and disheartening to recognize that nothing I’ve written has made one iota of difference. Trump continues to incorrectly dismiss climate science as a fraud. As a con job. As a hoax.

The real fraud is Donald J. Trump. The real hoax is in Trump’s efforts to persuade Americans that human-caused climate change is not happening. That wildfires are solely due to bad forest management. Or to Canadians. The real con job is in Trump’s repeated lies about global warming. That it isn’t happening. That all changes in climate are purely natural.

Trump is destroying so much that is good and valuable in America. He’s generating the very “American carnage” he described in his first inauguration speech. Carnage in pursuit of power, revenge, personal financial gain, and ego. He is remaking the country in his own image.

Now the National Academy of Sciences is firmly in his sights.

Why? Why does he care about an organization of scientists? A confederacy of nerds? Why does he care about climate science? Why does he believe, falsely, that climate science is fraudulent?

The National Academy of Sciences is on Trump’s radar because they are in his way. The climate science the National Academy of Sciences has assessed, for over four decades, is in fundamental conflict with Trump’s political agenda: the promotion of fossil fuels and the promotion of the powerful fossil fuel interests that have supported Trump’s rise. Science shows that fossil fuel burning is affecting Earth’s climate in harmful ways. So in Trump world, science is the enemy.

The cause of President Trump’s attack on the National Academy of Sciences is simple. The National Academy of Sciences is good at what it does. It has published reports on pretty much every aspect of climate science, most recently on what’s called “event attribution,” or the influence of human-caused climate change on extreme events.

Event attribution research provides hard evidence that fossil-fueled warming is ratcheting up the intensity and frequency of heat waves, and of extreme rainfall. This is the kind of evidence that may put fossil fuel companies on the hook for damages in lawsuits. As the tobacco industry learned decades ago, knowingly causing harm to human health can affect your corporate bottom line. The fossil fuel companies will eventually learn the same lesson.

But not under Donald Trump’s watch. He will do all he can to shield the Exxons and Chevrons of the world from accountability. If shielding means destroying the National Academy of Sciences, then so be it. If shielding means crippling the ability of this country’s leading institutions to monitor global warming, to study it with sophisticated computer models, and to understand the causes of warming, then so be it. If shielding means actively discouraging the use of cheap, efficient sources of low carbon energy, then so be it. If shielding means coming up with deeply flawed government reports that portray climate science as unsettled, then so be it.

President Trump doesn’t like bad news. Human-caused global warming is bad news. It’s bad news for his deep-pocketed supporters in the fossil fuel industry. It’s bad news for the narrative that under Trump’s tenure, everything is wonderful in America. It’s bad news for the fiction that the country’s future is bright.

But our future is not bright. It’s hot. It’s a future with lots of bad news and “downers.” Excess mortality from increasingly more intense heat waves is a downer. Larger, more intense wildfires are a downer, burning not only our forests, but also our cities, and leaving us choking in acrid smoke. Sea-level rise is a downer, taking billions of dollars off the value of coastal real estate.

This is why Trump is so exercised about the National Academy of Sciences. He doesn’t want event attribution reports. He doesn’t want fast-track reports assessing the evidence for human effects on global climate. He doesn’t want US courts to have a climate science chapter in the Reference Manual on Scientific Evidence, which provides judges with credible, vetted information about the reality, seriousness, costs, and causes of climate change.

It’s said that Nero fiddled while Rome burned. Others have argued he actually started the fire, so that he could rebuild the city to his liking. We cannot allow our American Nero to fuel the flames while the planet burns with his reckless pro-fossil fuel policies. And we cannot allow him to destroy institutions—like the US National Academies of Science, Engineering, and Medicine—that provide a candle in the growing darkness of ignorance.

In return, we promise our coverage will be understandable, influential, vigilant, solution-oriented, and fair-minded. Together we can make a difference.

item.title: Record Ocean Heat Raises New Concerns for Global Agriculture and Food Production
item.description:
Record Ocean Heat Raises New Concerns for Global Agriculture and Food Production

Sea surface temperatures have remained at record highs for more than 50 consecutive days, increasing the risk of extreme weather and adding uncertainty to crop production worldwide.

Sea surface temperatures have remained at record levels for more than 50 consecutive days, an unprecedented pattern for this time of year that is drawing increasing attention from climate scientists and agricultural analysts alike. Observed during the Northern Hemisphere summer of 2026, the sustained warming confirms that the world's oceans continue absorbing most of the excess heat generated by global warming. For agriculture, the implications extend far beyond the coastline: warmer oceans can reshape rainfall patterns, intensify extreme weather events and create greater uncertainty for crop production across major farming regions.

The world's oceans cover more than 70% of Earth's surface and absorb roughly 90% of the excess heat trapped by greenhouse gases. That makes them one of the most reliable indicators of long-term climate change. When ocean temperatures remain well above historical averages for weeks, scientists interpret it as evidence that the global climate system is operating from a much warmer baseline than it did only a few decades ago.

Warmer Oceans Mean Greater Uncertainty for Farmers

Sea surface temperature is far more than an environmental statistic. It influences evaporation, atmospheric moisture, storm formation and global circulation patterns that ultimately determine where and when rainfall occurs.

As oceans warm, they release additional heat and moisture into the atmosphere, creating conditions that can strengthen heavy rainfall events in some regions while increasing drought risk in others. For farmers, this growing climate variability complicates planting decisions, crop management and harvest planning, particularly in areas already vulnerable to water stress or extreme weather.

Scientists emphasize that while global warming remains the primary driver of this trend, natural climate patterns such as El Niño can further redistribute heat from the Pacific Ocean into the atmosphere, amplifying weather anomalies across multiple continents.

The persistence of these record temperatures is especially significant because it suggests a structural change rather than a short-lived weather fluctuation.

Climate Risks Extend Beyond Agriculture

The impacts are already visible across marine ecosystems. Coral bleaching events, shifting fish populations and changes in ocean biodiversity are becoming increasingly common as warmer waters alter marine habitats and fisheries.

For agriculture, however, the consequences may be even broader. More frequent heavy rainfall can delay planting and harvesting operations, while prolonged heat waves and irregular precipitation place additional stress on crops and livestock. Regions dependent on seasonal rainfall could experience greater production volatility, increasing uncertainty for producers and commodity markets.

Major agricultural exporters-including the United States, Brazil, Argentina, Canada and Australia-closely monitor ocean temperatures because they influence the atmospheric patterns that shape growing conditions across some of the world's most productive farming regions.

A Climate Signal Agriculture Cannot Ignore

Ocean temperatures have become one of the most closely watched indicators for anticipating seasonal climate behavior. As the planet continues storing more heat in its oceans, agricultural businesses, commodity traders and policymakers are paying greater attention to these signals when assessing production risks and market outlooks.

For the global food system, the challenge extends beyond adapting to warmer conditions. It increasingly requires anticipating greater climate variability, investing in resilient production systems and improving weather intelligence to reduce exposure to extreme events.

As agriculture faces mounting pressure to produce more food under increasingly unpredictable conditions, record ocean heat is no longer simply an environmental concern-it has become a strategic variable for global food production, commodity markets and long-term agricultural resilience.

item.title: Phivolcs sign partnership on enhanced climate risk management - The Manila Times
item.description:
STATE-OWNED Development Bank of the Philippines (DBP) has signed a memorandum of agreement with Department of Science and Technology (DOST-Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology) to integrate hazard information into the bank’s risk management, policies and processes, and optimize its lending and investment operations, a top official said.

DBP President and CEO Michael de Jesus said the agreement would allow the bank to access and harness the agency’s hazard information platform, GeoRiskPH, to ensure evidence-based credit evaluations and enable data-driven business decisions.

“We view this partnership with Phivolcs as a tangible manifestation of how government agencies can strengthen their collaboration and leverage shared expertise in advancing a safer, more resilient, and sustainable Philippines,” de Jesus said.

DBP is the ninth largest bank in the country with total assets of P1.041 trillion and provides credit support to four priority sectors of the economy — infrastructure and logistics; micro, small and medium enterprises; the environment; and social services and community development.

GeoRiskPH, a science-based platform led by Phivolcs, is a centralized government initiative designed to provide real-time data and risk analysis to support geohazard mapping and vulnerability assessments, helping strengthen disaster preparedness across the country.

Under the agreement, Phivolcs would provide DBP free access to the GeoRiskPH platform, including its HazardHunterPH Pro application, to enable the bank to manage the potential impact of natural hazards to its loan collaterals and investments.

“We believe that this initiative not only contributes to the broader goal of disaster risk reduction but also strengthens the Bank’s institutional resilience, especially in financing projects that would generate economic activity, particularly in the countryside,” de Jesus said.

item.title: Southern China faces torrential rain, flood risk after Typhoon Noul hits land
item.description:
Typhoon Noul will dump heavy to torrential rains across much of southern China for two days, authorities said, after sweeping the province of Guangdong and neighboring Hong Kong with gale-force winds, following landfall on Sunday.

China declared its highest alert for flash floods in several provinces as the year's strongest typhoon forced the relocation of more than 700,000 people in Guangdong, authorities said.

The year's 12th tropical cyclone and China's third this month, Noul, which means the glow of sunrise or sunset in Korean, struck the coast of Huidong county at about 3:50 a.m., provincial officials said.

It is expected to bring strong winds and heavy rain to nearby provinces such as Jiangxi and Hunan as it moves inland, state broadcaster CCTV said, with the rains likely to persist until Tuesday.

Extremely heavy to exceptional downpours are expected to lash some areas including the province of Fujian, as the National Meteorological Center forecast heavy to torrential rain from Sunday until Monday morning across much of China's south.

Typhoon weakening as it moves inland

Authorities urged local governments to pay special attention to flood-prone areas such as mountainous and riverine zones, building sites, valleys, and bridges.

The typhoon is weakening as it moves inland, Hong Kong's Observatory said, though southwesterly gales pounded parts of the Asian financial hub, where authorities downgraded the typhoon signal to No. 3 from No. 8 by afternoon.

Overnight, the storm had passed within 80 km of Hong Kong.

Hong Kong airport authorities said flights will gradually resume on Sunday afternoon, after being mostly suspended for more than 12 hours.

item.title: Trump Blames Canada For Smoke From A Climate America Created - CleanTechnica
item.description:
Trump Blames Canada For Smoke From A Climate America Created

Support CleanTechnica's work through

a Substack subscription,

on Patreon, or

on Stripe. Help us produce all of the

high-quality, original content we publish week after weekdespite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.

Donald Trump says Canada is poisoning American cities with wildfire smoke. He has told Prime Minister Mark Carney to get the fires under control, demanded compensation and threatened tariffs because smoke from Canadian fires crossed into the United States. The smoke did come from trees burning in Canada. That establishes the immediate source of the pollution, but says very little about the larger causes of the conditions producing fires of this scale.

The border tells us where the forests caught fire. It does not allocate responsibility for the hotter and drier conditions that have made North American wildfire seasons longer, larger and harder to control. Trump is treating the location of the burning trees as though it settles the climate question. It does not.

From 1850 through 2024, the United States produced about 24% of cumulative global fossil CO₂ emissions. The current EU27 produced about 16%, China 15% and India 4%. The United States has held the largest cumulative national total since 1917. A separate peer-reviewed assessment of national contributions to warming from historical CO₂, methane and nitrous oxide also puts the United States first.

China now emits more CO₂ annually, a comparison frequently used to divert attention from the cumulative nature of carbon dioxide. The climate influencing current wildfire conditions was not created by emissions from the latest reporting year. It was built over generations. The United States industrialized early, consumed fossil fuels on an exceptional scale, organized transport and land use around oil, and received enormous economic benefits from doing so. No individual country contributed more to the accumulated warming now affecting forests across the continent.

The fires are in Canada. The climate conditions affecting them are not exclusively Canadian, and the United States has contributed more to those conditions than any other country.

Climate attribution science does not claim that carbon dioxide starts individual fires. It examines how warming changes the conditions in which fires start and spread. Higher temperatures dry vegetation and soils, intensify drought, lengthen fire seasons and increase the probability that fires will grow beyond the capacity of suppression systems. Climate change does not have to increase the number of ignitions dramatically to produce much greater damage. It can do so by increasing the area capable of sustaining large fires and extending the period during which they can burn.

The peer-reviewed attribution analysis of Canada’s catastrophic 2023 fire season found that human-caused climate change more than doubled the likelihood of an area burned that large in eastern and southwestern Canada. It made an exceptionally long fire season more than five times as likely and increased the likelihood of simultaneous extreme fire weather across widely separated regions. Canada did not experience a record number of ignitions. The exceptional outcome came from fires becoming unusually large, persistent and geographically widespread.

There is not yet an event-attribution study assigning a precise climate fraction to the fires burning this week. That means a precise fraction should not be invented. It does not mean the established relationship between warming and severe Canadian wildfire conditions should be ignored until a paper addressing this exact event is published. Scientific caution about a particular percentage is not evidence that the broader causal relationship is uncertain.

Trump’s compensation demand therefore reverses the more important responsibility. The United States is not merely an uninvolved neighbour receiving pollution produced entirely by another country’s choices. It is the largest historical national contributor to the warming that has increased the likelihood and severity of this class of disaster.

Under any serious system of transboundary climate accountability, the United States would face far larger claims arising from its historical emissions than it could plausibly make against Canada for wildfire smoke.

The American responsibility is not confined to emissions released by people who died generations ago. The United States continues to make political choices that protect fossil fuel production and weaken climate policy. In 2016, the Electoral College installed Trump despite his losing the popular vote. In 2024, Americans returned him to office with 312 electoral votes and 49.8% of the national popular vote after having already seen his approach to climate science, environmental regulation and fossil fuel development.

There was little room for misunderstanding the second time. Americans had watched repeated megafires, smoke emergencies, heat waves, floods and billion-dollar disasters. They had seen Trump withdraw the United States from the Paris Agreement during his first term. They knew he opposed greenhouse gas regulation, promoted expanded fossil extraction and treated climate policy as an obstacle to economic growth.

Many voters ranked immigration, inflation, cultural grievance, partisan loyalty or gasoline prices above climate stability. That is their democratic right. It does not remove responsibility for the foreseeable climate consequences of the government they selected. Elections produce governments with entire policy programs, not individually chosen menu items. A voter may not have supported Trump because of his climate policies, but those policies were neither concealed nor incidental.

Enough Americans approved of them, accepted them or considered them unimportant enough to overlook that Trump returned to power. Since then, his administration has again withdrawn the United States from the Paris Agreement. His EPA has rescinded the 2009 greenhouse gas Endangerment Finding and repealed federal greenhouse gas standards for light-, medium- and heavy-duty vehicles. The federal government is weakening measures intended to reduce future climate risk while blaming Canada for failing to contain one of its consequences.

This does not make every American equally responsible. Children with asthma did not vote for the administration. Millions of Americans voted against it. Noncitizens could not vote, and lower-income households with poor access to filtration will often suffer more than wealthier people with greater political influence and better protection from smoke.

Those inequities matter, but they do not eliminate collective political responsibility. Governments act in the name of countries, national emissions accumulate regardless of internal political disagreement, and elections determine which policies will be pursued. Americans who opposed Trump’s climate agenda can accurately say they fought against it. The United States as a political community cannot claim that the choice was never made.

Canada deserves no general climate absolution. It is a wealthy, high-emitting fossil fuel producer whose governments have protected oil and gas production while repeatedly missing climate targets. Canadian emissions in 2024 were still 685 MtCO₂e, only 10.3% below 2005 and 12.6% above 1990. Oil and gas emissions were 5.1% higher than in 2005, while Canada’s own projections show current policies falling well short of its 2030 commitment.

Canada also has direct responsibility for protecting communities, improving evacuation systems, funding firefighting capacity, using Indigenous-led cultural fire where appropriate and managing fuels around settlements. Some losses will reflect inadequate preparation, poor land management or delayed responses by Canadian governments.

Those failures do not make the two countries equally responsible for climate change, and they do not turn the United States into an innocent downwind victim. Canada’s smaller population does not excuse its high per-capita emissions or fossil fuel expansion. Equally, Canada’s failures do not erase the much greater absolute historical contribution of the United States.

Nor can Canada extinguish every fire across the boreal forest simply because smoke is moving toward American cities. Canada contains millions of square kilometres of forest, much of it remote and sparsely populated. Lightning storms can create many simultaneous fires, including fires that become very large before crews can reach them. Attempting to suppress every remote fire would be physically impossible, ecologically damaging and extraordinarily expensive. The relevant questions concern preparation, priorities and protection of communities, not the fantasy that a national government can prevent a continental forest system from burning.

Trump’s argument depends on treating the border as decisive when smoke moves south and irrelevant when greenhouse gases move north. The atmosphere recognizes neither distinction. American emissions spread globally, contributed substantially to continental warming and helped intensify the conditions in which Canadian forests now burn. Canadian smoke is returning through that same shared atmosphere.

The United States is breathing smoke from Canadian fires. It is also experiencing a climate risk that it did more than any other country to create and that its voters have again chosen not to treat as a governing priority. Blaming Canada may be politically convenient, but it does not survive contact with the emissions record, attribution science or the policies Americans knowingly put back into office.
